items.label: Fig. 1: null case, p = 40, no selection; PA, PA1, PA2 against k1train (nine classifiers)

assumptions.what: Each simulated data set is a training set of 80 and separate test sets drawn from the same distributions, with round(80 k1train) Class 1 samples; the paper splits 100 samples into 80 and 20.
Random seeds: one per setting and replicate (from the setting's name); the paper's seeds are not given.

Replicates: 1,000 per setting, as in the paper, for the null case at p = 40 and the alternative case at p = 1000 (Figs 1 and 5's first column, Additional files 1, 3 and 11); 500 for every other setting and 200 for Additional file 6 and the hypothesis tests (compute budget). The tolerance uses our replicate count and the paper's.
Ties: DLDA and DQDA give ties to Class 1 (as sma::stat.diag.da); k-NN breaks ties at random (class::knn); PLR breaks ties at 0.5 at random (as stated).
RF: randomForest defaults (500 trees, mtry = sqrt(p)) with classwt = the training class proportions, as stated; RF-THR classifies as Class 1 when the vote share exceeds k1train.
SVM: e1071::svm, linear kernel, scale = FALSE, class.weights = the training class proportions (as stated) and the default cost 1 (not stated).
PAM: pamr.train with its default 30 thresholds; the largest threshold with the smallest training error (as stated).
PLR: stepPlr::plr with lambda = 1 (as stated), Class 1 coded 1.

AUC scores: share of neighbour votes (k-NN), difference of the two discriminants (DLDA, DQDA), vote share (RF), decision value (SVM), posterior (PAM), fitted probability (PLR). The paper says only that Hmisc was used.

A predictive value has no value in a replicate whose denominator is 0 (PV1 when PA1 = 0 and PA2 = 1). Means are over the replicates where the value exists; a cell the paper prints as NA or NaN counts as equal when some of our replicates have no value.

Published values are read from the vector figures: the paper's markers and the supplements' polyline vertices, mapped through each panel's tick marks (largest tick-fit residual below 0.0002 in y); points within 0.0005 of ours count as equal for reading error.

Monte Carlo tolerance: |ours - paper| <= printed + z sqrt(se_ours^2 + se_paper^2), se = SD / sqrt(replicates), with the paper's SD where printed and ours otherwise, the paper's 1,000 (500 for the breast cancer data) replicates, and z the Bonferroni value for a 5% chance of any false miss in the item.

cause.summary: (1) SVM: the paper gives no cost, and its class weights ('the proportion of samples from each class') leave the direction open. With the default cost 1 our SVM is less biased than the paper's in the simulations (Additional file 3, k1train 0.1: PA1 0.18 against 0.03; there the weights change nothing at cost 1). A smaller cost with the stated weights brings Additional file 3 back (cost 0.1: 0.08; 0.03: 0.00) but sends the null case of Fig. 2 to 0 (cost 0.1: 0.001 against 0.038). On the breast cancer data the stated weights go the wrong way (20 ER+ / 5 ER-, PA ER-: 0.46 at cost 1 against 0.6); weights inverse to the class sizes with cost 0.1 give 0.60 there but 0.56 at 45 ER+ / 5 ER- (paper 0.49). Weights taken from the original rather than the over-sampled training set change nothing (Additional file 8, k1train 0.1: PA1 0.22 and 0.22). No cost and weighting of the grid fits all of them. (2) PAM without correction: our PAM is slightly more biased than the paper's near balance in the null case (Fig. 1, k1train 0.45: PA1 0.23 against 0.27) and at 45 ER+ / 5 ER- (PA ER- 0.47 against 0.53). The paper says the threshold was the one with the smallest training error, not which one of the ties. The smallest tied threshold gives 0.24 and 0.47; 10-fold CV 0.09 and 0.56; equal class priors 0.46 and 0.63. None fits both. Without variable selection (Additional file 6) the difference runs the other way: the paper's PAM puts nearly every sample in the majority class (k1train 0.2: PA 0.52), ours less so (0.73). (3) Values near 0 or 1: a few points where our replicates are all or nearly all 0 or 1, so the Monte Carlo tolerance is close to 0, and the paper's values differ from ours by less than 0.003.

cause.summary: p = 40 and pDE = p: the paper says the samples were centred, and with centring our minority-class PA is far below the paper's where 20 of 40 or all of the variables differ (9 of 156 such points of Fig. 3 match, 32 of 171 of Additional file 4, 27 of 297 of Additional file 5). Centring the samples over 40 variables of which half or all are shifted removes most of the signal. Rerunning these settings without centring (200 replicates) matches 155 of 156 points of Fig. 3, 112 of 171 of Additional file 4 and 254 of 297 of Additional file 5; what still misses is the SVM, PAM at pDE = p, and the k1train = 0.95 end at pDE = 20, where the paper's PA1 is a little lower than either of our runs. Our run keeps the stated centring.

cause.summary: (1) Over-sampling, overall PA: Fig. 5's over-sampling PA is the PA of a test set as imbalanced as the training set (k1 PA1 + (1 - k1) PA2 from our class-specific means: 50 of 57 points match, against 19 for the balanced test set the caption implies), while Additional file 8, which repeats the panel for all classifiers, uses the balanced test set (109 of 171 against 59). The two figures disagree; we compare with the balanced test set. (2) Over-sampling, order of selection: with variables selected on the original training set and the classifier fitted on the over-sampled one, DLDA's and DQDA's PA at k1train 0.2 is 0.88 and 0.79 (paper: 0.88, 0.79); selecting on the over-sampled set, which the Methods describe and our run does, gives 0.85 and 0.74. The k-NN classifiers move little either way (3-NN 0.86 / 0.85). (3) Values near 0 or 1: a few points where our replicates are all or nearly all 0 or 1, so the Monte Carlo tolerance is close to 0, and the paper's values differ from ours by less than 0.003.

assumptions.what: Data: the BRB-ArrayTools project of Sotiriou et al. (2003) in the NCI BRB data archive; its RawData, ProcessedLog and FilteredAndNormalizedLog arrays are identical (median-centred log ratios); missing values set to 0, as stated.

Each of the 500 draws per design takes the training samples and 20 test samples per class without replacement from the ER+ and ER- tumours; class 1 is ER+; predictive values use the training proportion of ER+.
Fig. 6 and Additional file 12 draw the designs at their ER+ share (50, 66.7, 80, 85.7, 90% with 5 ER-; 50, 66.7, 75, 81.8% with 10 ER-); each plotted point is matched to the nearest design.
assumptions.sensitivity: The nearest design is at least 4 points of ER+ share away from the next; a wrong match would put a point 5 or more points off in x.

assumptions.what: Over-sampling draws the max(n1, n2) - min(n1, n2) replicated minority samples with replacement; down-sizing keeps min(n1, n2) majority samples drawn without replacement.
MultDS: 101 down-sized sets, t-test selection of 40 variables inside each, majority vote (as stated). At k1train = 0.5 no sample is left out, so all 101 classifiers are the same.
Variable centering is applied to the training set the classifier is fitted on (after over- or down-sizing, inside each MultDS set) and to the test set separately.
Predictive values use the original training proportion (k1train), also after a correction.

Published values are read from the vector figures: the paper's markers and the supplements' polyline vertices, mapped through each panel's tick marks (largest tick-fit residual below 0.0002 in y); points within 0.0005 of ours count as equal for reading error.

Monte Carlo tolerance: |ours - paper| <= printed + z sqrt(se_ours^2 + se_paper^2), se = SD / sqrt(replicates), with the paper's SD where printed and ours otherwise, the paper's 1,000 (500 for the breast cancer data) replicates, and z the Bonferroni value for a 5% chance of any false miss in the item.
Prediction-interval ends are our 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles over replicates (R's quantile type 7); with a 20-sample test set they move in steps of 0.05, and they count as equal within one step.

cause.summary: Prediction intervals: a few interval ends miss by two steps of 0.05, nearly all lower ends at the smallest training sets (377 of 382 ends of Fig. 6 and 930 of 976 of Additional file 12 match). The lower 2.5th percentile of 500 draws rests on its 13 lowest values, which the paper's draws (unknown seeds) and ours place differently. Other interval definitions fit worse: mean -/+ 1.96 SD matches 310 and 703, 5th and 95th percentiles 361 and 893.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The intervals are mean -/+ 1.96 SD

Replicates: 1,000 per setting, as in the paper, for the null case at p = 40 and the alternative case at p = 1000 (Figs 1 and 5's first column, Additional files 1, 3 and 11); 500 for every other setting and 200 for Additional file 6 and the hypothesis tests (compute budget). The tolerance uses our replicate count and the paper's.
Ties: DLDA and DQDA give ties to Class 1 (as sma::stat.diag.da); k-NN breaks ties at random (class::knn); PLR breaks ties at 0.5 at random (as stated).
RF: randomForest defaults (500 trees, mtry = sqrt(p)) with classwt = the training class proportions, as stated; RF-THR classifies as Class 1 when the vote share exceeds k1train.
SVM: e1071::svm, linear kernel, scale = FALSE, class.weights = the training class proportions (as stated) and the default cost 1 (not stated).
PAM: pamr.train with its default 30 thresholds; the largest threshold with the smallest training error (as stated).
PLR: stepPlr::plr with lambda = 1 (as stated), Class 1 coded 1.

AUC scores: share of neighbour votes (k-NN), difference of the two discriminants (DLDA, DQDA), vote share (RF), decision value (SVM), posterior (PAM), fitted probability (PLR). The paper says only that Hmisc was used.

A predictive value has no value in a replicate whose denominator is 0 (PV1 when PA1 = 0 and PA2 = 1). Means are over the replicates where the value exists; a cell the paper prints as NA or NaN counts as equal when some of our replicates have no value.

Published values are read from the vector figures: the paper's markers and the supplements' polyline vertices, mapped through each panel's tick marks (largest tick-fit residual below 0.0002 in y); points within 0.0005 of ours count as equal for reading error.

Monte Carlo tolerance: |ours - paper| <= printed + z sqrt(se_ours^2 + se_paper^2), se = SD / sqrt(replicates), with the paper's SD where printed and ours otherwise, the paper's 1,000 (500 for the breast cancer data) replicates, and z the Bonferroni value for a 5% chance of any false miss in the item.

cause.summary: (1) SVM: the paper gives no cost, and its class weights ('the proportion of samples from each class') leave the direction open. With the default cost 1 our SVM is less biased than the paper's in the simulations (Additional file 3, k1train 0.1: PA1 0.18 against 0.03; there the weights change nothing at cost 1). A smaller cost with the stated weights brings Additional file 3 back (cost 0.1: 0.08; 0.03: 0.00) but sends the null case of Fig. 2 to 0 (cost 0.1: 0.001 against 0.038). On the breast cancer data the stated weights go the wrong way (20 ER+ / 5 ER-, PA ER-: 0.46 at cost 1 against 0.6); weights inverse to the class sizes with cost 0.1 give 0.60 there but 0.56 at 45 ER+ / 5 ER- (paper 0.49). Weights taken from the original rather than the over-sampled training set change nothing (Additional file 8, k1train 0.1: PA1 0.22 and 0.22). No cost and weighting of the grid fits all of them. (2) DQDA's AUC: lower than the paper's when the training set is imbalanced (k1train 0.1: 0.87 against 0.91). The paper does not say which score it ranked. Ranking by the ratio of the two discriminants instead of their difference gives the paper's AUC at every k1train (0.91, 0.98, 0.99, 0.99, 0.99) and moves DLDA's AUC only from 0.94 to 0.95 at 0.1 (paper 0.94); the predictions do not change. Found by search over five scores; our run keeps the difference.

cause.summary: (1) SVM: the paper gives no cost, and its class weights ('the proportion of samples from each class') leave the direction open. With the default cost 1 our SVM is less biased than the paper's in the simulations (Additional file 3, k1train 0.1: PA1 0.18 against 0.03; there the weights change nothing at cost 1). A smaller cost with the stated weights brings Additional file 3 back (cost 0.1: 0.08; 0.03: 0.00) but sends the null case of Fig. 2 to 0 (cost 0.1: 0.001 against 0.038). On the breast cancer data the stated weights go the wrong way (20 ER+ / 5 ER-, PA ER-: 0.46 at cost 1 against 0.6); weights inverse to the class sizes with cost 0.1 give 0.60 there but 0.56 at 45 ER+ / 5 ER- (paper 0.49). Weights taken from the original rather than the over-sampled training set change nothing (Additional file 8, k1train 0.1: PA1 0.22 and 0.22). No cost and weighting of the grid fits all of them. (2) PAM without correction: our PAM is slightly more biased than the paper's near balance in the null case (Fig. 1, k1train 0.45: PA1 0.23 against 0.27) and at 45 ER+ / 5 ER- (PA ER- 0.47 against 0.53). The paper says the threshold was the one with the smallest training error, not which one of the ties. The smallest tied threshold gives 0.24 and 0.47; 10-fold CV 0.09 and 0.56; equal class priors 0.46 and 0.63. None fits both. Without variable selection (Additional file 6) the difference runs the other way: the paper's PAM puts nearly every sample in the majority class (k1train 0.2: PA 0.52), ours less so (0.73).

cause.summary: (1) SVM: the paper gives no cost, and its class weights ('the proportion of samples from each class') leave the direction open. With the default cost 1 our SVM is less biased than the paper's in the simulations (Additional file 3, k1train 0.1: PA1 0.18 against 0.03; there the weights change nothing at cost 1). A smaller cost with the stated weights brings Additional file 3 back (cost 0.1: 0.08; 0.03: 0.00) but sends the null case of Fig. 2 to 0 (cost 0.1: 0.001 against 0.038). On the breast cancer data the stated weights go the wrong way (20 ER+ / 5 ER-, PA ER-: 0.46 at cost 1 against 0.6); weights inverse to the class sizes with cost 0.1 give 0.60 there but 0.56 at 45 ER+ / 5 ER- (paper 0.49). Weights taken from the original rather than the over-sampled training set change nothing (Additional file 8, k1train 0.1: PA1 0.22 and 0.22). No cost and weighting of the grid fits all of them. (2) PAM without correction: our PAM is slightly more biased than the paper's near balance in the null case (Fig. 1, k1train 0.45: PA1 0.23 against 0.27) and at 45 ER+ / 5 ER- (PA ER- 0.47 against 0.53). The paper says the threshold was the one with the smallest training error, not which one of the ties. The smallest tied threshold gives 0.24 and 0.47; 10-fold CV 0.09 and 0.56; equal class priors 0.46 and 0.63. None fits both. Without variable selection (Additional file 6) the difference runs the other way: the paper's PAM puts nearly every sample in the majority class (k1train 0.2: PA 0.52), ours less so (0.73).
